tagline.text: A red-brick lighthouse from 1896 overlooking the Verde Island Passage

children.text: This Spanish-era lighthouse, completed in 1896, stands on a cliff in Lobo, the southernmost part of Batangas. It is still run by the Coast Guard and is a National Historical Landmark, with a pebble beach and the Verde Island Passage spread out below.
Malabrigo Point Lighthouse (Faro de Punta Malabrigo) stands in Barangay Malabrigo in the municipality of Lobo, Batangas. It lies about
115km

southeast of Manila and has long guided ships through the Verde Island Passage toward Batangas Bay or the Sibuyan Sea. It is one of the lighthouses built under the Spanish colonial government's maritime lighting plan (1846–1896).
It was designed in 1891 by the Spanish engineer Guillermo Brockman and built of brick and lime cement by a company led by the Chinese contractor Jose Garcia, and it was first lit on
October 1, 1896
. It is a Victorian-inspired round brick tower with a metal staircase, a double balcony, keeper's quarters and a machine room. The tower is about
tall and the light sits about
above sea level. The tower and lantern are now painted red.

The name Malabrigo is said to come from the Spanish for "bad shelter," because the rocky coast and the strong monsoon currents made this a dangerous place for sailors. The lighthouse was declared a National Historical Landmark by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) and is still an active light run by the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG). In 2014 the Lobo municipal government signed an agreement with the Coast Guard to adopt it and carried out repairs and repainting, and today it is counted among the best-preserved lighthouses in the country. A staircase links the lighthouse and the pebble beach, so you can walk down and look around at your own pace.

Historical records note that the US Navy vessel Villalobos guarded the lighthouse from 1900 to 1902 during the Philippine–American War, and that during World War II Japanese forces occupied it and its top was damaged by machine-gun fire from advancing American troops. After a film crew shot there without permission in 2006 and caused some damage, filming has required a permit from the Lobo Mayor's Office. In 2016 a Coast Guard patrol vessel was also named BRP Malabrigo.
It is a Victorian-inspired lighthouse with a round brick tower, a metal staircase and a double balcony. The contrast between the red walls and the blue sea makes it the biggest draw for photos.

It originally used a first-order Fresnel lens, but the lens was damaged and was replaced by a bulb when the light was automated in 1980. In 1994 a solar-powered halogen light was installed with a loan from Japan's JICA. The light can be seen from about
28km
away and repeats a signal of three flashes every 15 seconds.

blocks.title: Views of the Verde Island Passage

children.text: From the cliff you look down on the Verde Island Passage and the sea toward Mindoro Island on the other side. On clear days the view opens to the horizon, which is great for sunrise and sunset photos. Watching the large ships pass through the strait is also fun.

On the cliff side below the lighthouse is a beach covered with gray and white pebbles instead of sand. The water is said to be very clear, and you can walk down from the lighthouse by a zigzag staircase.

blocks.title: Malabrigo mini park and viewing deck

children.text: On the way to the lighthouse there is a small park and viewing deck overlooking the palm-fringed sea. It is a good place to stop and take photos before you reach the lighthouse.

blocks.title: A national landmark and film location

children.text: The NHCP designated it a National Historical Landmark, and it has also been a location for several Philippine films and TV dramas. Filming requires permission from the Lobo Mayor's Office.
If you drive about
6km
along the Lobo coast, you can see high waves and wide-open sea views. The road is unpaved and rocky, so slow down.

items.title: Day trip from Manila
items.subtitle: The lighthouse and the pebble beach

children.text: Take a bus bound for Batangas City from Manila (Cubao, Pasay or Alabang). If there is no traffic it takes about
3 hours
Get off at the Batangas Grand Terminal, take a jeepney toward SM City Batangas, then go to Lobo town proper from the Lobo jeepney stop. Ask locally to find the stop.
Hire a tricycle in Lobo town proper to go to Malabrigo. It is about
6km
and takes about
10–20 minutes
. Arrange your ride back at the same time.
Look out over the sea from the mini park and viewing deck by the road, then look around the lighthouse exterior and its surroundings.
Take the stairs down to the pebble beach and walk along the water. Bring aqua shoes if you want to swim.
Have lunch and rest at a nearby resort. Some accept day visitors, but you need to check the conditions locally.
Take a tricycle back to Lobo town proper and a jeepney to Batangas City. Be sure to check the last jeepney and bus times.
Public transport schedules vary by season and day of the week. Be sure to check the last jeepney and the last bus to Manila in advance.

items.title: Two days, one night
items.subtitle: Enjoying the lighthouse and the sea

children.text: Reach Malabrigo the same way as on the day trip and look around the lighthouse and the pebble beach.
Check in to a resort on the Malabrigo beach side and watch the sunset from the beach and the coastal cliffs.
Go out around the lighthouse at sunrise to see the morning view of the strait. The Parish Church of Saint Michael the Archangel (Lobo Church) in Lobo town proper is also worth a stop.
If you want to snorkel or dive, ask about the coral garden in Barangay Sawang. Then return to Batangas City by tricycle and jeepney.

items.title: By bus and jeepney from Manila

children.text: Take a bus bound for Batangas City from Cubao, Pasay or Alabang in Manila and get off at the Batangas Grand Terminal. It takes about
3 hours
, depending on traffic.
From the terminal, take a jeepney toward SM City Batangas and transfer to a jeepney bound for Lobo town proper at the Lobo jeepney stop.
It is about
6km
from Lobo town proper to Malabrigo Lighthouse, and since there is no regular public transport, you hire a tricycle.
Some travelers report that buses with a CALABARZON sign on the windshield are faster. When boarding, confirm with the driver that the bus stops at the Batangas Grand Terminal.

items.title: By private car or rental car from Manila

children.text: Take the southern expressways (SLEX and the STAR Tollway) from Manila past Batangas City to Lobo town proper, then continue on to Malabrigo. It is about
from Manila to Lobo.
The road to Malabrigo is unpaved and rocky, but vehicles can get through. In the rainy season, check the road condition locally.

items.title: By tricycle from Lobo town proper

children.text: A tricycle hired from Lobo town proper to the lighthouse is reported at about
one way. Arrange your ride back with the driver in advance.
Some stretches are sloped, so it is easier to go early in the day.
The drier season from December to about May is a good time to visit (the rainy season sets in from June). The sea is calm and the sky is clear, which helps with views and photos.

April and May overlap with the Philippine school break, so weekends and holidays are crowded. For a quieter visit, go early on a weekday. In the rainy season, monsoon currents and waves can be rough, making beach and sea activities difficult.

On the Malabrigo beach side, lodgings such as Punta Malabrigo Beach Resort and Punta Verde Dive Resort are known. Some accept day visitors or let you use shower facilities, but conditions change often, so contact them before you go.

Lobo town proper has small eateries and shops, and an ATM as well. There are few shops near Malabrigo, so it is wise to bring water and snacks. Cash is the easiest way to pay, and reports say Globe and Smart signals both work.

On a day trip you can eat lunch in Lobo town proper before heading in, or use a resort restaurant near Malabrigo. Menus and opening vary by day, so do not count on them and bring snacks. Do not enter private villas or private land that are not resorts.
The easiest plan is to leave early in the dry season, see the lighthouse in the morning and head out in the afternoon.
Agree on a return time with your tricycle driver in advance. There may be no vehicle waiting permanently in front of the lighthouse.
The stones on the pebble beach can get hot in the sun, so wear aqua shoes or thick sandals.
There is little shade, so bring sunscreen, a hat, sunglasses and water.
Bring plenty of cash in small bills. Many places outside Lobo town proper do not take cards.
This is not for anyone expecting a sand beach. It is a pebble beach.
Drone and film or video shooting may require permission. Commercial filming requires permission from the Lobo Mayor's Office.
Take your trash back with you and do not damage the lighthouse or the coastal nature.
Malabrigo Point Lighthouse is an active navigational aid. Entry to the tower and photography may be restricted by Coast Guard and municipal policy, so follow local instructions.
There is no regular public transport to the lighthouse, so you can be in trouble if you cannot secure a ride back. Check the time of the last jeepney from Lobo in advance.
The access road is unpaved, rocky and sloped, so it can be slippery after rain.
Around the cliff and the coastal stairs, be careful not to fall while taking photos near the edge.
In the rainy and typhoon seasons the waves and currents are strong, so do not swim on the strait side.
Prices, operating arrangements and permit rules can change, so check the latest notices.
This island lies across the Verde Island Passage, in the waters the lighthouse's beam watches over. Check boat services and schedules locally.
It is the transfer point on the way to Lobo and the end of the line for buses. It has the Grand Terminal and the port.

blocks.title: Lobo town proper and the church

children.text: In Lobo town proper, about
6km

from Malabrigo, stands the Parish Church of Saint Michael the Archangel (Lobo Church). The patron saint Michael's feast day is said to be May 8, and the town's foundation-day festivities are held in late September.
A coral garden suited to snorkeling and diving is said to be there. Lobo also has fish sanctuaries, including Malabrigo, Biga and Sawang.
